heading: 1 Introduction / 1.1 Problem Background and Restatement
note: 8 blocks, 8 groups. Block 23 is the last three lines of the table of contents ('7 Sensitivity Analysis 22 8 Strengths and Weaknesses 23 8.1 Strengths ... 8.2 Weaknesses ...') with the '1 Introduction 1.1 Problem Background and Restatement' headings glued to its tail, so the chapter text begins at 24. 24-25 are pure motivation with no quantity ('space resources should also be utilized by all mankind. Among them, asteroid mining is an important part of developing space resources' / 'The promotion and realization of asteroid mining will have a great impact on the development of all countries and will greatly change the international structure'). 26 is the lead-in ('Based on this background, this paper needs to solve the following problems:') and 27-30 are the four task statements, one measured block each, so the four jobs are four separate routes rather than one merged group. 30's tail carries '1.2 Literature Review'. The restatement is verbatim from the problem statement and its wording is the paper's only definition of scope.

heading: 1.2 Literature Review
note: 2 blocks, 2 groups. 31 gives the whole review in three sentences and a figure pointer: 'research on this topic is very hot.Generally, it can be divided into 3 parts: the strategies of asteroid mining, the impacts of asteroid mining, regulation and legal regime of asteroid mining. We can see the framework from Figure 1.' No individual study is named, no citation number appears in the block, and the three branches are never worked through — the chapter delegates its entire content to the figure. 32 is the 'Figure 1: Literature Review Framework' caption and carries the '1.3 Our Work' heading in its tail. This is the thinnest literature review in the queue so far: the bibliography (pp. 24-25, eleven entries) exists but is attached to the body at points of use, not traced here.

heading: 1.3 Our Work
note: 12 blocks, 6 groups. A four-item work summary built as numbered list items split one printed line per block: item 1 (34-36) 'a Global Equity Assessment Model is established.Then we select raw data for 25 indicators of 205 countries and regions'; item 2 (37-39) the asteroid mining model 'from four aspects:preparations,mining process, sale, allocation and impacts', applied to 2011UW-158; item 3 (40-41) throughput factor and country count; item 4 (42) policies. 43 is the flowchart pointer ('In order to intuitively reflect our work process, the flow chart is shown in Figure 2.') and is grouped with 44, the 'Figure 2: Flow Chart of Our Work 2 Assumptions and Justifications' caption whose tail carries the next chapter's heading — so the group is read-figure and the chapter ends on it. The 25-indicator / 205-country / four-aspect counts stated here are the paper's own scope declaration and are taken up again verbatim in chapter 3 (25 indicators) and section 4.4 (2011UW-158).

heading: 2 Assumptions and Justifications
note: 20 blocks, 6 groups: a lead-in and five assumption/justification pairs, each pair split over 2-5 measured blocks because the justification wraps line by line. (1) mining is 'technically feasible, and financially worth the investment' — 'This is the basis for the whole model.'; (2) 'Only a few countries ... will have the relevant technology' — justified as a route into Cournot-Nash equilibrium; (3) actors are rational and maximise utility — justified only by tractability ('the complexity of calculation will be greatly increased'); (4) mining will be done by private companies with possible state investment, justified on the US Commercial Space Launch Competition Act; (5) 'Our data sources are reliable and accurate' — justified circularly ('Since our data comes from international data sites, we assume that the data is reliable'). Every job is limit, not derive, because no assumption is tested or quantified; assumption 5 is the one the sensitivity analysis later tries to buy back with gaussian noise. Block 64's tail is '3 Model I: Global Equity Assessment Model'.

heading: 3 Model I: Global Equity Assessment Model (definition and requirements)
note: 7 blocks, 4 groups. 65 is the section heading and 66 delivers the paper's one sentence definition: 'The definition of Global Equity: provision of varying levels of support and assistance based on specific needs or abilities, to achieve greater fairness of treatment and outcomes.' — a needs-adjusted definition, which is why the later index weights asset and achievement separately. 67 is the requirement lead ('The model ... should meet the following requirements:') and 68-69 give universal coverage ('applicable for most countries'), 70 comprehensiveness, 71 robustness ('The evaluation results of the model are relatively stable in the case of possible uncertainty') with the '3.1 The Capability Approach' heading in its tail. All three requirements are promises at this point; only robustness is ever tested (section 7, gaussian noise).

heading: 3.1 The Capability Approach / 3.2 Individual Welfare Assessment
note: 10 blocks, 6 groups. 72 opens on the theory and hands off in the same block ('In the 1970s, Amartya Sen put forward the perspective and analysis method of the capability approach ... 3.2 Individual Welfare Assessment'); no citation number is given for Sen. 73-74 build the country-level bridge and the assumption it needs: 'if the individual welfare situation in different countries is basically the same, we can assume that the situation in these countries is also basically the same' — this is the load-bearing inference of the whole model, and 74's tail carries the 'Figure 3: Evaluation System Logic' caption. 75-81 define individual welfare as two capital types: capital held by the individual (76-77: 'individual economic situation, resources occupied, labor force') and disposable capital provided by the environment (78-81: 'science and technology, education and medical treatment ... national trade, national military reserve'). 81's tail carries '3.3 Global Equity Assessment'. The split of the two capital types is what later appears as 'asset' (held) versus 'achievement' (output).

heading: 3.3 Global Equity Assessment / 3.4 Global Equity Assessment Model
note: 7 blocks, 5 groups. 82 sets the three-category frame ('We need to consider the following variables in a country-level analysis of global equity, which can be divided into three categories') and 83-84 define two of them with a single line each: 'Asset, that is, the ability of a country to invest' and 'Achievement, namely, the output effect obtained by the country after the initial investment'. 85-86 define the third ('Group differences mainly refer to cross-country group differences and some other factors ... (a) Gender Difference') and 87-88 carries '(b) Peace Factors' plus the stacked heading fragments '3.4 Global Equity Assessment Model 3.4.1' and 'Determination of Indicators and Data Collection' — two headings and a sub-heading glued across two blocks with no prose, so the pair is a route group. Note the mismatch of granularity: asset and achievement get one sentence each while group differences gets two named components, and only the latter two are later measured by an external index (GDI, peace index).

heading: 3.4.1 Determination of Indicators / 3.4.2 Data Normalization
note: 8 blocks, 6 groups. 89 announces the indicator set through a figure ('The secondary and tertiary indicators of asset and achievement are shown in Figure 4.') and 90 is its caption — the 25 indicators are never listed in text, so the indicator list exists only in the raster. 91 names the data provenance: 'we collect data through authorization data, including Our World in Data and World Bank' (source job; the bibliography's [9] and [10] are the two sites, [6] the World Bank report). 92 states the normalisation scheme ('we process 25 indicators and normalize the data through forward processing. These 25 indicators can be divided into two categories: benefit attributes and cost attributes') and 93-94 are the two min-max formulas, split so that each formula straddles a block boundary. 95-96 point to Figure 5 for the attribute classification and carry the '3.4.3' heading fragment. Nothing in this chapter is numeric beyond the count 25; the actual values and the attribute list live in figures 4 and 5 only.

heading: 3.4.3 Calculate Weights - Entropy Weight Method(EWM)
note: 9 blocks, 7 groups. 97-98 give the heading and the rationale ('the smaller the information entropy of an index is, the greater the variation degree of the index value is, the more information it can provide'). 99-102 are the four EWM steps with the formula at the end of each block and its gloss at the start of the next: Step 1 pij normalisation, Step 2 ej = -K Σ yij ln yij, Step 3 wi = (1-ej)/Σ(1-ej), Step 4 the weight statement — four derive groups, matching the standard EWM chain exactly. 103 is the weight output and it is a figure, not a table: 'After analyzing the existing data, we get the following weight table. Figure 6: The Indicators' Weights' — so no weight value appears anywhere in the text layer of the paper, and the 25 weights cannot be audited from prose. 104-105 give the scoring formula S = 100 Σ yij wj and gloss S and wj. The 'figure 6' label is later mis-referenced in 4.3.5 (block 157) where 'As shown in Figure 6' points at the investment-split result.

heading: 3.4.3 (cont.) Group differences: GDI, peace index, and the CV of EI
note: 14 blocks, 7 groups. 106 introduces the Gender-related Development Index and states its provenance ('according to the UNDP Human Development Report'); 107-114 are three cited GDI findings, each split one printed line per block: 'no country in the world has achieved the ideal state of gender equality (GDI=1), and only 44 out of 173 countries had a GDI of more than 0.8 in 2002'; gender equality 'could be pursued at any income level'; and 'GDI and GEM values have increased in all countries, and no country has regressed'. 115-116 are the paper's own number and the only computed value in the group: 'the current gender development index is 0.721 < 0.8 that is to say, gender inequality is still quite significant' — the 0.721 is not derived from 44/173 and the year of 'current' is never given. 117 turns to war and terrorism and says a peace index is 'calculated' from 'the latest global research reports' without naming a source or a formula. 118-119 build the composite and the equity statistic: EI per country, then 'CV = σEI / µEI' with the gloss that CV measures the dispersion of EI and therefore global equity — so the paper's entire equity verdict is one coefficient of variation over 205 country scores, and 119's tail carries '3.5 Model Validation 3.5.1 Regional Analysis'.

heading: 3.5 Model Validation (3.5.1 Regional, 3.5.2 Historical)
note: 11 blocks, 7 groups. 120 states the regional test ('draw two global scoring heat maps') and 121-123 are the two captions plus the pointer sentence ('As shown in figure 7 and figure 8.'), grouped because the captions alone say nothing. 124 is the whole regional reading — 'areas with higher asset scores tend to have higher achievement scores. North America and Europe are leading the way.' — and is also where the '3.5.2 Historical Analysis' heading sits. 125-126 give the 2000 pair (asset CV 1.2437, achievement CV 0.5766) and 127 the 2020 pair (1.5332, 0.6912); these four numbers are the only internal validation statistics in the paper. 128 reads them ('the degree of dispersion has become larger, the gap between the rich and the poor has intensified') and 129 appeals to the World Bank's World Development Report 2020 for external support, 130 adds the drivers and closes on 'This also verifies the credibility of our model.' Note the validation is of direction only: both CVs rise, which the paper treats as confirming the model, but any monotone aggregate would do the same — nothing checks the absolute level of either CV.

heading: 4 Model II: Asteroid Mining Model / 4.1 Exploiting Countries and Funding Countries
note: 11 blocks, 6 groups. 131 is the '4.1' heading grouped with 132, the GE/McKinsey selection scheme: ten countries and regions scored on GDP per capita and aerospace capability, the latter taken from 'Beijing Institute of Space Science and Technology Information' across 'five dimensions: government support, technological capac(ity)...'. 133-134 are the pointer and the 'Figure 9: Five-dimensional Aerospace Competitiveness Evaluation' caption; 135 normalises both axes to [0,1] and carries the 'Figure 10: GE Matrix' caption in the same block, so it is its own read-figure. 136 is the reading ('the United States has the highest score in both ... Russia, Japan and India all need financial support'), 137-139 are conclusion 1 (mining countries: 'the United States, Europe, China, Russia, Japan and India') and 140-141 conclusion 2 with the '4.2 Selection of Target Asteroids' heading in 141's tail. No score, weight or threshold is printed for the GE matrix — the three-tier split into miners, funders and neither is read off a raster with no cut values, and the same split is used again unexamined in 5.2.

heading: 4.2 Selection of Target Asteroids
note: 6 blocks, 6 groups. 142 gives the spectral taxonomy (C, S, X, 'the X category is mainly composed of metallic asteroids, especially the M-type'); 143-145 are one block per class with the literature's abundance figures: C-type 'accounts for about 75% of all asteroids', S-type '17% of all asteroids' plus 'one part per million of platinum group elements', M-type 'a high proportion of gold and platinum group elements'. These three are source groups because every figure is external and no citation is printed beside them (the citation [5] arrives only with the Figure 11 caption in 147). 146 is the selection rule and it is purely qualitative: 'Different asteroids have different characteristics and values, so we need to choose according to the needs of mining.' 147 is the 'Figure 11: Overview and Main Applications of Small Celestial Bodies Resources[5]' caption with '4.3 Process of Asteroid Mining 4.3.1 Cost' in its tail. 75% + 17% leaves 8% unaccounted for across the three classes the paper says are exhaustive.

heading: 4.3.1-4.3.4 Cost, Mass Collected, Total Time, Net Present Value
note: 9 blocks, 6 groups. 148 takes the cost from the Keck Institute white paper ('the effort would cost about 2.6 billion dollars') and 149 rounds it up: 'we can make a reasonable estimate that the cost of asteroid mining is about 3.0 billion dollars' — a 15% uplift with no stated reason; this 3.0 bn is the denominator of every profitability statement later. 150-151 give the mass model Mi = ρ·(4/3)π(D/2)^3·Ei·TP with the gloss for ρ, D, Ei and TP ('the ratio of the collected mass to the total amount of the substance'). 152-153 give T = T1 + T2 + T3 with the three phases glossed. 154 anchors the time in a real mission ('Based on the sampling time of Hayabusa2 to Ryugu(1999 JU3) ... the total time T is about 4 years, of which the mining season is about 160 days[7]') — note the 4-year figure is a round-trip at Hayabusa2's scale, and no velocity or delta-v model stands behind it. 155-156 give the NPV with I, It and R glossed. Every symbol chain here is complete (formula then gloss), unlike the orphaned glosses in the other F papers of 2022.

heading: 4.3.5 International and National Responsibilities
note: 9 blocks, 7 groups. 157 allocates the burden and mis-points its evidence: 'As shown in Figure 6, when investing in asteroid mining, Russia, Japan and India need to attract foreign investment while the United States, China and Europe have the ability to invest by themselves' — Figure 6 is the indicator-weight figure on p. 10; the intended target is the GE matrix (Figure 10). 158-159 introduce the ME-MI model from [4] with 'two decision variables as minimum investment amount(I) and rate of return(ROR)'; 160-161 bring in the Hotelling distance and print dis = sqrt((xf-xi)^2 + (yf-yi)^2); 162 glosses x, y as I and ROR and the subscripts as actual versus expected; 163 states the satisfaction rule as three cases in I and ROR ('degree = 0, when ROR/I >= 2; degree = 2 - ROR/I, when 1 < ROR/I < 2; degree = 1, when ROR/I <= 1') — note the middle case gives degree 0 at ROR/I = 2 and 1 at ROR/I = 1, so the scale is inverted relative to the first and third cases and the rule is not monotone. 164 is Tables 1 and 2 (US and China department duties) in a single measured block, hence one read-figure; 165 reads the contrast ('Private enterprises in the United States are involved in the mining of asteroids, while private enterprises in China are not').

heading: 4.3.6 Sale in Oligopoly Market
note: 16 blocks, 7 groups. Three characteristics are asserted to justify the market form, each split one printed line per block: limited number of capable suppliers (166-168), irreplaceable supply (169-171), rational actors selling 'at a price higher than the original price ... in batches by year' (172-173), with 174 concluding 'By the above three characteristics, we can think that this is an oligopoly market.' 175-176 give the linear demand p = a - bm; 177-178 the profit eta_i = p(sum m_i)m_i - c m_i; 179-180 the Cournot equilibrium m_i = (a - c)/((n+1)b) — the standard symmetric solution, correctly printed, and the only place n (the oligarch count) enters the model. 181 states the distribution rule in words only ('If the government carries out mining, the government will keep some of the collected materials ... If there is an investor ... the investor will participate in the profit sharing') with no share parameter — so section 5's country-count experiment must be inferring shares from the A-D tiers rather than from this rule.

heading: 4.3.7 Impacts / 4.4.1 The Background of Asteroid 2011UW-158
note: 11 blocks, 5 groups. 182 splits impacts into direct (sale revenue, and state-retained material affecting national resources) and 183 supplies the indirect channels — political ('if the United States is willing to cooperate with other space nations, it will be able to establish an international legal and institutional framework'), geopolitical and environmental — and carries the '4.4 Analysis ... 4.4.1' heading fragments in its tail. 184-189 are the case dossier, split one printed line per block: '2011UW-158 is a X-type asteroid. It is less than 1km in diameter but is considered to be of great value due to its platinum core', a target of 'Planetary Resources'. 190 sets the throughput factor for the case ('we set TP to be 1/200') and 191 carries the 'Figure 12: 2011UW-158' caption; 192 closes the case setup with the headline number: 'a single mining operation on this asteroid would be worth about 27 billion dollars'. Against the 3.0 bn cost of 149 that is a ~9x gross return, and the paper never discounts it: the NPV formula of 155-156 is printed and never applied, so 27 bn is a gross value compared to a gross cost.

heading: 4.4.2 Data Analysis of the Impact of Mining 2011UW-158
note: 12 blocks, 8 groups. 193-194 start the analysis ('we will take a mining activity as an example'). 195 narrows the treated set to three actors ('only the United States, China and Europe have the ability to complete asteroid mining independently') — this contradicts the GE-matrix reading of 136-139, which put Russia, Japan and India in the mining group, and the later 5.2 experiment puts them back in as 'second level'; 196 is the impact channel ('reap huge economic benefits ... which will have a huge impact on their GDP, while the impact on other aspects is small and can be ignored'). 197 is the correlation screen with the 'Figure 13: Variable Correlation Diagram' caption inside the block. 198 states the cutoff ('For variables with correlation coefficients(R∗) greater than 0.3, we conducte multiple linear regression'), 199-200 are Table 3 in one block: ST, TR, EN, MR, PMS against GDP and LR, e.g. ST = 0.319077 GDP + 0.039535 LR - 0.01267, TR = 0.52139 GDP + 0.053327 LR - 0.0194, EN = -0.2691 GDP - 0.22625 LR + 0.963858, MR = 0.422633 GDP + 0.074996 LR + 0.008554, PMS = 0.227677 GDP + 0 LR + 0.030809. 201-203 restate five of these as equations and the restatement drops the constant on the last one ('byPMS = 0.2227677xGDP + 0.227677'): the PMS constant 0.030809 is missing and the GDP coefficient is misprinted 0.2227677 for 0.227677, so anyone reusing the printed equations inherits two errors. 204 is the outcome: 'the coefficient of variation of asset is 1.5379, and the coefficient of variation of achievement is 0.6945, which change from the data of 1.5332 and 0.6912 when no asteroid mining is conducted' — asset +0.0047, achievement +0.0033, both tiny against the 2000-2020 drift of +0.2895 and +0.1146 that the paper called a widening gap.

heading: 4.4.3 The Conclusion Obtained from the Analysis of Mining
note: 4 blocks, 3 groups. 205 is the heading with 206, the reading rule ('if the average level of variable value is high, the measure value of its dispersion degree is larger, and vice versa') and its application ('the coefficients of variation for both assets and achievements increased ... the gap between the rich and the poor around the world has widened'). 207 supplies the mechanism at individual level ('the popularity of asteroid mining has made the well-being of individuals in the United States, China and Europe even better, further exacerbating the gap') and 208 is the chapter verdict plus the '5 Analysis of the Changes in Our Asteroid Mining Model' heading: 'As a result, asteroid mining has exacerbated global inequity.' The verdict rests on the fourth-decimal increments of 204, and the caveat printed in 206 cuts both ways — since CV scales with the mean, a mining-driven GDP rise would raise CV even with unchanged relative dispersion, which is exactly the confound this chapter does not separate.

heading: 5.1 The Throughput Factor is Higher
note: 11 blocks, 7 groups. 209 is the section lead ('we take into account two factors: the throughput factor of target collection and the countries participating in asteroid mining') with the 5.1 heading in its tail, and 210 states the channel. 211 is the perturbation: 'we assume that the throughput factor becomes four times and ten times as high as before' — two points only, no curve. 212 points at Figure 14 and 218 is its caption, so the pointer and the caption are separate read-figure groups with the numbers between them. 213-215 give the 4x case: achievement CV '0.6945 to 0.6946' and asset CV '1.5379 to 1.5383'; 216-217 give the 10x case: 0.6945 to 0.6948 and 1.5379 to 1.5388. So a four-fold rise in throughput moves the achievement CV by 0.0001 and a ten-fold rise by 0.0003, while the mining event that produced the baseline moved it by 0.0033 — ten times larger. 219 is the reading ('the increase of throughput factor(TP) makes ... CV higher, and do harm to global equity'), which is directionally what the arithmetic gives but on changes two to three orders of magnitude smaller than the effect it is compared with.

heading: 5.2 More Countries Join Asteroid Mining
note: 9 blocks, 5 groups. 220 is the tier definition that the experiment rests on: 'first level ... the United States, China, and Europe ... second level countries: India, Japan, and Russia, and the third level countries: Canada, South Korea, Israel and Australia ... as shown in the GE Matrix (Figure 10)' — ten countries in three tiers, read off the same raster. 221-223 are the second-level run (achievement 0.6945 -> 0.6937, asset 1.5379 -> 1.5375), 224-225 the third-level run where 'The achievement coefficient of variation(CV) doesn't change' and asset goes 1.5375 -> 1.5359. 226-227 are the pointer and the 'Figure 15' caption. 228 is the reading and the '6 Policy Setting' heading: 'the increase in the number of countries entering the asteroid mining market makes the achievement and asset coefficient of variation(CV) lower and promotes global equity.' The asymmetry is worth recording: adding three tier-2 countries moves achievement by 0.0008 and then adding four tier-3 countries moves it by exactly 0.0000, so the second half of the claim (that tier-3 entry promotes equity) is carried entirely by the asset CV, while the second-level entry — the one the GE matrix supports with scores — is the only one that moves achievement at all.

heading: 6 Policy Setting (6.1 Restrict, 6.2 Encourage, 6.3 Supervise)
note: 23 blocks, 13 groups. 229 frames the chapter ('we propose a series of policy suggestions for the renewal of the Outer Space Treaty'). Each of the three subsections has a rationale paragraph followed by numbered policies split one printed line per block, so each policy becomes its own hand-off group: 6.1 restrict private companies — rationale 230 (monopoly risk, consumer welfare) and policies on treaty coverage of private actors (231-233), national regulation (234-235), shared state-company responsibility (236-237); 6.2 encourage exploitation — rationale 238-239 ('as more countries enter ... global equity will be improved', which is the 5.2 result used as the warrant) and policies on property-right clarity (240-242), an international information platform (243-244), state-company cooperation (245-246); 6.3 strengthen supervision — rationale 247 (space-economy conflict risk), policies on activity registration (248) and a militarisation ban (249-250). That is eight numbered policies, matching the abstract's '8 policy suggestion'. 251 is the 'Figure 16: The Framework of Policy' caption carrying the '7 Sensitivity Analysis' heading, hence read-figure. Every policy traces to a result except 6.1's monopoly argument, which cites the oligopoly model rather than any measured CV; no policy carries an instrument, cost, or enforcement mechanism.

heading: 7 Sensitivity Analysis
note: 3 blocks, 3 groups. 252 states the threat honestly ('the data is slightly different because it comes from different sources. Fluctuations of the data may affect the weights determined by the entropy weight method') — this is the only test aimed at assumption 5. 253 is the perturbation design ('we add some gaussian noise to the raw data ... we calculate the relative error of weights with the standard deviation of gaussian noise increasing') with the 'Figure 17: Gaussian Noise Curve' caption in the same block. 254 gives the result and the verdict: 'when the standard deviation of gaussian noise is no more than 0.8, the relative error of the weights does not exceed 5%. So we conclude that data errors and fluctuations have little effect on weights ... our Global Equity Assessment model is credible and stable.' The threshold pair (0.8 noise, 5% error) has no calibration argument — 0.8 is not stated in data units, so the reader cannot tell whether it is a large or small disturbance relative to the normalised indicators.

heading: 8 Strengths and Weaknesses
note: 7 blocks, 5 groups. Four claims, one per strength, in the order comprehensive / objective / credible / robust: 255 counts the three-level indicator system plus the inclusion of 'the effects of sexism and war'; 256 credits the entropy weight method with removing subjective weighting; 257 argues credibility from full process coverage, the 2011UW-158 case and the correlation screen ('we exclude the influence of correlation among indicators through correlation test'); 258 argues robustness from section 7. 258's tail carries '8.2 Weaknesses' and 259-261 are the three limitations: country-level aggregation ('we analyse the country as a whole, which affects the accuracy of the model'), the idealised assumptions forced by 'the lack of complete asteroid mining practices', and the absence of any quantitative treatment of 'political environment, spatial economy and other factors'. 261's tail carries 'References' followed by eleven entries on pp. 24-25, which are inside this block's boundary but are not a coded chapter. The weakness list omits the two things a reader would flag: the CV-versus-mean confound in 206 and the fact that every weight lives only in Figure 6.
